title: Scanning Old Family Photos and Slides at Home: Two Scanners, Plus a Film Alternative
subtitle: A plain-English guide to picking the right home scanner for boxes of prints or trays of slides, and what each one cannot do.
excerpt: Shoeboxes of prints and carousels of slides can become digital files you can share and back up. Here is how to choose between a flatbed photo scanner and a slide-and-negative scanner, with no rush.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Almost every family has them: a shoebox of curling prints in the hall closet, an album with photos slowly fading to orange, or a stack of slide trays nobody has seen projected since the 1980s. Those pictures are one flood, move or spilled cup of coffee away from being lost for good.

A home scanner turns those originals into digital files, so they can be copied, shared with grandchildren and stored safely. It can also make a thoughtful gift at any time of year, especially when a family helper offers to sit down and scan alongside Mom or Dad.
Prints and slides need different scanners
The first question is what you are scanning. Paper prints and film (slides and negatives) are handled by different machines, and one usually cannot do the other's job.

A flatbed scanner works like a small copy machine. You lay a print face down on the glass, close the lid and press a button. It is slow, one photo at a time. A bulk or feeder scanner pulls stacks of prints through faster, though it can be harder on old, brittle photos.
"Bulk scanners are best for people with a lot of old materials they want scanned." — NBC News Select, December 26, 2025

A film scanner is a small box for slides and negatives. You load the film using its slide and film inserts, press one button, and it saves a picture to a memory card. These do not scan paper prints at all.

One honest note: scanning does not fix a blurry original. A higher dpi number (dots per inch, a measure of detail) mainly makes bigger files, not sharper old photos. For do-it-yourself scanning, Consumer Reports has suggested a free app such as Adobe Scan or an all-in-one printer, which can give higher-quality scans and let you crop photos individually.

items: Match the machine to the material. Prints need a flatbed; slides and negatives need a film scanner. Check which film sizes are listed, such as 35mm, 110 or 126.
Count the hidden costs. The Kodak models do not include an SD memory card, and the Slide N Scan is powered from USB or a 5V/1A power adapter, which is not included.
Look for one-touch buttons, which keep the steps simple.
Check for subscriptions. None of the products below showed a monthly fee on its product page.
Think about hands. Loading small slides into trays can be fiddly; a family helper can do the loading.
Check the seller's return policy before giving one as a gift. We have not checked any of these policies, and it matters if the recipient's photos turn out to be a different format.
Be realistic about time. A collection of 500 prints on a flatbed is several evenings of work. For very large collections on a deadline, a professional scanning service may make more sense.

sections.content: Setting it up and scanning well
Start small. Pick one album or one slide tray rather than the whole closet. A common-sense tip: handle prints and slides gently, and keep your hands clean.
Make it a visit. Scanning goes faster with two people, one loading and one jotting down who is in each picture. Those stories are worth capturing while you have them.
Finally, decide where the files will live. A scanner only creates the pictures; keeping them safe is up to you.

Save every scanned photo in two places, such as the computer plus an external drive or a cloud storage service. A single copy is not a backup. If you are giving a Kodak scanner, tuck an SD card in with the gift so it works right away.
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: These old photos are often the most treasured things a family owns. With a modest scanner and a few patient evenings, you can make sure they outlast the shoebox and reach the people who will cherish them next.

products.name: Epson Perfection V19 II Color Photo and Document Flatbed Scanner
products.blurb: For families with paper prints and albums: lay each photo on the glass and press one button, with 4800 dpi optical resolution, Easy Photo Fix to restore faded colors and a high-rise lid for bound albums. It is powered by USB and does not scan slides or negatives.

products.name: KODAK Slide N Scan Film & Slide Scanner Digitizer with 5" LCD Screen
products.price: $189.99 regular price (Kodak Photo Plus, November 2026); check current price, as the site also lists $179.99
products.blurb: For drawers of slides and negatives: it handles 35mm, 110 and 126 film plus 50mm slides, with a 5-inch screen, one-touch scanning and no computer software needed. The SD card and 5V/1A power adapter (if you don't power it from USB) are not included, and it does not scan prints.

products.name: KODAK SCANZA Digital Film & Slide Scanner
products.blurb: A lower-priced film-only alternative to the Slide N Scan that also accepts Super 8 and 8mm film alongside 35mm, 126 and 110, with a 3.5-inch tilt-up screen and one-touch buttons. Its screen is smaller, the SD card is not included, and it does not scan paper prints.
